root_cause.text: In the sched/rt root_domain overload selection logic, rto_next_cpu() did not exclude the currently executing CPU, so when rd->rto_loop_next changes forced a restart of the scan, an already overloaded CPU could reselect itself and repeatedly queue self-IPIs.
root_cause.evidence: The patch adds `int this_cpu = smp_processor_id();` and `if (cpu == this_cpu) continue; /* Do not send IPI to self */` inside `rto_next_cpu()`, while the CVE/commit explains that mismatches between `rd->rto_loop` and `rd->rto_loop_next` caused the search to restart and reselect CPU0, leading to infinite self-IPI loops and hardlockup.

commit 4bdced5c9a2922521e325896a7bbbf0132c94e56
Author: Steven Rostedt (Red Hat) <rostedt@goodmis.org>
Date:   Fri Oct 6 14:05:04 2017 -0400

    sched/rt: Simplify the IPI based RT balancing logic
    
    When a CPU lowers its priority (schedules out a high priority task for a
    lower priority one), a check is made to see if any other CPU has overloaded
    RT tasks (more than one). It checks the rto_mask to determine this and if so
    it will request to pull one of those tasks to itself if
bic_trace_step.reason: The snippet shows the relevant root-domain overload iteration logic directly, especially `rto_next_cpu()` and `rto_push_irq_work_func()`, so it is sufficient to judge. The vulnerable construct is present because `rto_next_cpu()` scans `rd->rto_mask` using `cpu = cpumask_next(rd->rto_cpu, rd->rto_mask);` and, on restart, resets `rd->rto_cpu = -1;` before re-reading `rd->rto_loop_next`. That means a restarted scan begins again from the first CPU in `rto_mask` with no exclusion of the currently executing CPU. In `rto_push_irq_work_func()`, after doing local push work on `rq = this_rq();`, it takes `rq->rd->rto_lock`, calls `cpu = rto_next_cpu(rq);`, and then unconditionally queues `irq_work_queue_on(&rq->rd->rto_push_work, cpu);` when `cpu >= 0`. Unlike the old code that explicitly handled self-selection (`if (unlikely(cpu == rq->cpu)) goto again;`), that protection was removed in this commit. Therefore, if `rto_loop_next` changes and forces a restart, an overloaded CPU can select itself again and queue another IPI to itself, matching the root cause. Since no logic here excludes `rq->cpu` / current CPU from `rto_next_cpu()` results and no replacement self-skip exists in `rto_push_irq_work_func()`, the fix is not present.

bic_trace_step.code_snippet:
commit 4bdced5c9a2922521e325896a7bbbf0132c94e56
Author: Steven Rostedt (Red Hat) <rostedt@goodmis.org>
Date:   Fri Oct 6 14:05:04 2017 -0400

    sched/rt: Simplify the IPI based RT balancing logic
    
    When a CPU lowers its priority (schedules out a high priority task for a
    lower priority one), a check is made to see if any other CPU has overloaded
    RT tasks (more than one). It checks the rto_mask to determine this and if so
    it will request to pull one of those tasks to itself if
bic_trace_step.reason:
The snippet is sufficient because it contains the full new root_domain RT overload iteration logic, including `rto_next_cpu()`, `tell_cpu_to_push()`, and `rto_push_irq_work_func()`, which are exactly where the described root cause would appear.

The vulnerable construct is present in `rto_next_cpu(struct rq *rq)`. The function does `cpu = cpumask_next(rd->rto_cpu, rd->rto_mask);` and returns that CPU whenever `cpu < nr_cpu_ids`, after assigning `rd->rto_cpu = cpu`. There is no check anywhere in this function to exclude the currently executing CPU (`rq->cpu` or `smp_processor_id()`).

This matters because the function also contains restart logic: when the scan reaches the end, it sets `rd->rto_cpu = -1`, reads `next = atomic_read_acquire(&rd->rto_loop_next);`, and if `rd->rto_loop != next` it does `rd->rto_loop = next` and loops again. With `rd->rto_cpu = -1`, the next iteration starts again from the beginning of `rd->rto_mask` via `cpumask_next(-1, rd->rto_mask)`. Since there is no exclusion of the current CPU, an overloaded CPU currently executing `rto_push_irq_work_func()` can select itself again on restart.

The caller `rto_push_irq_work_func()` then unconditionally queues work to the selected CPU: `cpu = rto_next_cpu(rq);` followed by `if (cpu < 0) return;` and then `irq_work_queue_on(&rq->rd->rto_push_work, cpu);`. Unlike the older removed code, there is no self-CPU avoidance such as `if (unlikely(cpu == rq->cpu)) goto again;`. The diff explicitly removed that old protection from the prior implementation.

Therefore this commit version contains the bug: it can reselect the current CPU during restart-driven rescans and queue self-IPIs repeatedly. The fix is not yet present because there is no logic in `rto_next_cpu()` or its caller to skip the current CPU during selection or to handle self-selection specially.
